# Pixels to Meaning: VLMs and VLAs

::: {.callout-question}

What does the scene mean, and who should decide, the device or the cloud?

:::

Detection tells you there is a mug and a hand. Meaning tells you the child is
reaching for the mug, the mug is the hot one, and the robot should say something
now. That leap, from objects to what they imply, is what a vision-language model
buys you, and it is the most expensive thing the robot does.

It is expensive enough that for the first time the placement is genuinely
contested. The reflex loop obviously belonged on the device. Meaning does not,
because the model good enough to read a scene may be too big to run on the robot
at all, which makes the cloud tempting in a way it never was before.

## Meaning is the expensive step

A model that names objects can be small. A model that understands a scene, that
grounds language in pixels well enough to say what is happening and what to do
about it, is large, because it has to carry a great deal of the world to do it.
That size is the whole tension. Run it on the device and you are limited to a
tiny model with rough judgment. Send the scene to the cloud and you can use a
model that reasons well, but the frame has to leave the room and an answer has to
return, and both legs of that round trip cost you.

::: {.column-margin}
**Properties in tension**: capability against latency, cost, and privacy. The
cloud buys the first by spending the rest.
:::

A useful way to keep the family straight: a VLM maps pixels and words to an
answer, and a vision-language-action model, a VLA, is a VLM whose output
vocabulary includes actions. The placement question is the same for both. Only
the stakes of a wrong answer change, because a VLA's answer moves the body. And
that answer is intent, not a motor command: like any decision it sets a target the
real-time control layer, the microcontroller, turns into safe motion, never driving the actuators
directly.

## The cost of asking the cloud

The placement turns on a comparison you can write down. Running meaning in the
cloud costs a round trip, not just an inference:

$$t_\text{cloud} = t_\text{upload} + t_\text{infer} + t_\text{download}$$

You weigh that against $t_\text{local}$, the single inference of whatever model
fits on the device. @fig-meaning-placement draws the two paths. The cloud path is
almost always slower, often by enough to miss a loop deadline, and it carries a
second cost the local path does not: every frame you upload is bytes leaving the
device, the same egress that the deployment chapter audits. In a child's room
that privacy cost can decide the placement on its own, before latency even enters
the argument.

::: {#fig-meaning-placement fig-cap="**Placing meaning**: the same frame can go to a tiny model on the device for rough meaning with nothing leaving, or to a large model in the cloud for rich meaning at the cost of a round trip and the frame itself." fig-alt="One frame feeds two paths. The top path sends it to a tiny VLM on the device, returning rough meaning in about 150 milliseconds with nothing leaving. The bottom path uploads it to a big VLM in the cloud, returning rich meaning in about 600 milliseconds, with the frame leaving the device."}
![](../assets/diagrams/meaning-placement.svg)
:::

## The grounding gap

Capability has a failure mode that latency and bytes do not capture. A VLM can be
fluent and confidently wrong, describing a scene it did not actually read, or
naming an object that is not there. The gap between what the model can say and
what is really in front of the camera is the grounding gap, and it is an
observability problem: the model gives you an answer but not its evidence, so you
cannot easily see when it has drifted from the scene. A bigger model narrows the
gap but never closes it, which is why a VLA's action always needs a safety floor
underneath it: not a simple safety cut-off that only catches a hung or garbled call, but
the control envelope that clips even a fluent, well-formed command to safe limits
before the body executes it. Capability is not the same as trust.

## Build

::: {.callout-build title="Ask both, then place the answer"}

Take one frame and one question about it, the kind the robot would actually ask,
such as "is the child reaching for something hot." Send it to a small model you
can run locally and to a capable cloud model. Compare three things: the quality
of the two answers, the latency of each, and the bytes that left the device for
the cloud call.

Before you measure, predict. Estimate $t_\text{local}$ from the model size and
$t_\text{cloud}$ from your upload bandwidth and a typical inference time. Then
defend a placement in one sentence, naming the budget that decided it.

A capable on-device VLM may be too heavy for the board you have, which is the
real constraint, not a gap in the exercise. If so, use the provided local-model
latency numbers and run only the cloud call live; the decision is still yours to
make and defend.

:::

## What the number says

Two surprises are common. The local model is often good enough: the question the
robot actually needs answered is narrower than the open-ended one the big model
was built for, and a small model aimed at that narrow question can clear the bar.
And the cloud answer's latency is dominated by the round trip, not the inference,
so a faster model in the cloud barely helps while a closer one would. The lesson
is the placement, not the leaderboard. You put meaning where the binding budget,
usually privacy or latency, says it belongs, and you reach for the cloud only when
the task truly needs a capability the device cannot hold.

## Read

The grounding of language in images traces to CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), and
the action-output models this chapter folds in include RT-2 (Brohan et al., 2023)
and the open OpenVLA; at the tiny end, models like SmolVLM and moondream are what
make the on-device path plausible at all. On-device execution runs through
runtimes such as ExecuTorch. The literature moves fast, but the placement question
it raises does not.

::: {.callout-teaching}

- **Hook**: ask the same image question of a tiny local VLM and a cloud VLM, and
  compare the answers and the latency side by side before any theory. The gap in
  both is the chapter.
- **Open question**: does a VLA deserve its own chapter, or is it a thread woven
  through chapters 2 to 4? For now the one-line framing ("a VLM whose outputs
  include actions") carries it.
- **Watch**: keep capability honest. It is easy to let the cloud model's fluency
  read as competence; the grounding gap is the reminder that it is not.

:::
